input:
The position is somewhat more subtle than it first appears. According to the Chilton-Colburn analogy, the mass-transfer factor is simply equal to half of the friction factor, so that $j_D = f/2$, at least in situations where the drag is of the skin-friction kind. The reason the two quantities can be linked in this way is that both of them are concerned with transfer at the surface: the friction factor reflects the momentum that is transferred to the wall, while $j_D$ reflects the mass that is transferred to it, and the analogy in effect treats these as two views of one and the same process. A simple numerical check illustrates the point: if the friction factor has been measured as $f$ = 0.008, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.004, and a value measured independently that came out very different from this would fall outside what the analogy can account for.

The difficulty arises when the drag is not purely skin friction. Where a body experiences form drag, part of what is captured in the measured friction factor has to do with the separated flow and the wake, and this part has no equivalent in the transfer of mass at the surface. The friction factor is then larger than the skin-friction value that the analogy presumes, and the $j_D$ worked out from it is correspondingly overestimated. The moral is that the analogy can only be trusted where the drag really is skin friction, and it should be set aside for geometries in which form drag makes a significant contribution to the measured factor.
target:
For flow over a surface where the drag is skin friction, the Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the mass-transfer factor equal to half the friction factor, $j_D = f/2$. The statement is compact because the two factors rest on the same surface process: the friction factor measures the momentum carried to the wall, and $j_D$ measures the mass carried to it, and the analogy asserts that the two standings are one. Neither factor is adjusted to reach the other; the equality is the content of the analogy. A check fixes the arithmetic of the claim. At a measured $f$ of 0.008, the analogy returns $j_D$ = 0.004, and a mass-transfer measurement that lands far from that value is a measurement the analogy does not describe.

The limit of the statement is the drag itself. Where the drag on the body is form drag, the friction factor counts momentum transfer that has no counterpart in the mass flux at the surface: the flow separates, the wake carries the momentum away, and $f$ stands above the skin-friction value the analogy assumes. The $j_D$ taken from such an $f$ is correspondingly high, and the error is not in the arithmetic but in the reading of $f$. The distinction is in what the measured drag is made of, and it is made before the analogy is applied, not after. The analogy is therefore used where the drag is skin friction, and set aside where the geometry puts form drag into the measured factor.
